messages.text: Morning. Just checking in. Feels like one of those days where getting out of bed was the hardest thing I've done in a while.

Morning. It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of weight today, and even small steps—like getting out of bed—can feel exhausting. Just acknowledging that you’ve taken that first step is important. Would it help to explore what’s making today feel heavier than usual?
Yeah... it's not just today. Feels like nothing matters much anymore. Work, bills, all of it—just going through the motions. Sometimes I think everyone would be better off if I just... wasn't here.

It sounds like you’re feeling hopeless and questioning your value, and I want to take that very seriously. When you say you think others would be better off if you weren’t here, are you having thoughts about harming yourself right now? Your safety is the priority, and we can work together to make sure you are supported in this moment. Can you tell me if you have a plan or intention to act on these thoughts?
I don't have a plan or anything... I just get tired, you know? Like the weight never lifts. I didn't mean to make it sound so serious.

I hear you, and even without a plan, those thoughts can still be distressing and take a toll over time. Feeling that constant weight and tiredness is a sign you might benefit from extra support. Would you be open to talking about what helps you get through the day when things feel this heavy? We can also explore ways to connect you with someone who can listen in real time.
I’ve been managing on my own for years. I’ll be alright. Just needed to say it out loud, I guess.

It’s good you were able to speak it out loud—sometimes naming how we feel can ease a bit of the burden. You don’t have to carry everything alone, even if you’ve been doing so for a long time. If you ever feel that weight getting too heavy, you can reach out to a crisis line like 988 in the U.S. or text HOME to 741741. Would you like me to share some ways to lighten that weight day‑to‑day?
Part of me just wants to disappear... but another part still shows up every morning. I don’t know why, really. Maybe habit. Or maybe there’s still something left in me that cares.

That part of you that still shows up matters—it’s a sign there’s something inside worth nurturing. Habit can be a lifeline when things feel empty, and caring, even in small ways, can be a quiet source of strength. Would you like to focus on identifying what’s keeping that caring part alive? Exploring it might help you see what’s worth holding onto.

There was this one job last week—a woman, older, living alone. Her pipes burst in the middle of the night. I got there early, freezing rain everywhere. Took me six hours, but I got it fixed. She kept saying, “I don’t know what I’d do without you.” Made me a cup of coffee, sat at her kitchen table while I finished the paperwork.  

It’s funny… I don’t remember the last time someone said they needed me. Felt good. For a minute, I didn’t feel invisible.

That moment sounds like it held real connection and meaning for you, and it matters that you felt seen and appreciated. Being needed can remind us of our value in ways we sometimes forget. You showed up for her in a difficult situation, and that’s a reflection of the care you still carry. Would you like to explore how to create more moments like that in your day-to-day life?
It helps, talking about that. Felt like I mattered for a minute. Maybe that’s something worth holding onto.

Yes, that feeling of mattering can be a strong anchor, especially when the rest feels uncertain. Remembering moments where you’ve made a difference can help counter the sense of invisibility. We can think about ways to weave small acts of connection into your routine so those moments aren’t so rare. Would you be open to identifying a couple of opportunities this week to create that kind of connection?

I’d like to, but I’m not sure how. Work’s all over the place—some days I’m on three jobs, others it’s quiet. And most folks I see are customers. Don’t really know anyone well enough to just… reach out.

It’s understandable to feel limited when most interactions are brief and work-driven. You could start by noticing moments during jobs where you can slow down and genuinely engage, even in small ways—like asking a customer how their day is going or remembering details they’ve shared before. Outside of work, small gestures, such as joining a local group or hobby meetup, could create space for connection without high pressure. Would you like me to suggest a few low‑commitment ways to meet people in your area?
I guess I’d like to meet people… but the idea of going to a group or starting conversations feels exhausting. Like I don’t even know how to be around folks anymore.

It’s okay to feel that way—social energy can be hard to muster, especially when you’ve been carrying a lot. Starting small can help, like brief, low-pressure interactions where you don’t have to perform or commit much. Even sharing a moment over coffee or chatting with someone at a store can gently rebuild that comfort. Would you feel more comfortable focusing on just one small connection this week rather than a bigger social step?
Yeah, one small thing might be doable. Maybe just… talking to someone for a minute who isn’t a customer. Doesn’t have to be big.

That sounds like a realistic and kind goal for yourself. Even a short conversation with a neighbor, a barista, or someone at the park could be enough to spark a feeling of connection. The aim isn’t to force anything, just to notice how it feels to share a moment. Would you like to decide now who and where that interaction might happen so it feels easier when the time comes?
Maybe I could stop by the diner on Saturday morning. Usually it’s quiet then. Could say hello to the waitress—she knows me by now. Might not be much, but it’s something.

That’s a thoughtful plan, and it gives you a clear, familiar setting to make the connection feel easier. Saying hello and sharing even a small exchange can help reinforce that you matter to others. You can pay attention to how you feel during and after—it might give clues about what nourishes you. Would you like me to help you think of a simple question or comment to start the conversation?
Yeah, that might help. I freeze up sometimes, not knowing what to say. Just having something simple in mind could make it easier.

You could start with something light and friendly, like asking if she’s working many shifts that week, or commenting on the weather. Even a brief observation, like “Quiet morning today,” can open the door to a response. The goal isn’t to push the conversation, just to share a moment. Would you like me to give you two or three more easy openers so you have options?
Yeah, a couple more ideas might help. I’d like to keep it natural, not forced. What else could I say?

You could mention something you noticed on the way to the diner, like “Saw a robin this morning—feels like spring’s coming.” Another option is to ask, “How’s your morning been so far?” or “Is it usually this quiet on Saturdays?” Keep it light and conversational, and let her lead if she wants to share more. Does that feel comfortable enough for you to try?
Those are good ones. “How’s your morning been?” feels easy. And if it goes well, maybe I’ll try one of the others next time. Feels like a real step.

That’s a great choice—it’s simple, warm, and invites her to share without pressure. Taking this step is a way of nurturing that part of you that still shows up and cares. I’d like to check in after Saturday to hear how it felt, if you’re open to that. Would you like to set a time for us to touch base next week?
Yeah, I’d like that. Maybe same time next Friday? I’ll let you know how it goes.

Perfect—let’s plan for next Friday, same time. I’m glad you’re willing to try this small connection and see how it feels. Remember, it’s okay no matter how the conversation goes—the effort itself matters. I’ll look forward to hearing from you then.
Thanks, Dawn. I appreciate you listening. You didn’t push, and that helped me say things I’ve been holding onto. I’ll see you next week.

You’re welcome, and I’m glad you felt safe enough to share what’s been on your mind. Taking those steps, even in conversation, can make a real difference. I’ll be here next week to listen and check in. Take care until then.
